title: Before: stock llama.cpp serving Qwen3.8-Flash-Next
subtitle: One token's trip through a 111 GB model on 2×3090 + 62 GB RAM + one NVMe, drawn like a database's storage tiers

nodes.label: You
nodes.desc: Sends a prompt and waits for tokens.

nodes.label: Router
nodes.desc: The query planner: for every token and every layer it picks which 10 of 512 experts (rows of weights) to read.
nodes.notes: Database view: each expert is a 3 MB page; a token is a query that touches 480 pages.

nodes.label: GPU 0
nodes.desc: Runs attention, the shared parts and the experts of the layers that fit in its memory.

nodes.label: GPU 1
nodes.desc: Same, for the next block of layers.

nodes.label: CPU
nodes.desc: Computes the experts of the 24 layers (of 48) that did not fit on the GPUs, straight from RAM. Measured: 24 layers' experts here.
nodes.notes: It waits while the GPUs work and the GPUs wait while it works: the two take turns.

nodes.label: VRAM 0
nodes.desc: Holds whole layers' experts, chosen by layer number, not by use.

nodes.label: RAM page cache
nodes.desc: The operating system caches the expert file here. The CPU-tier experts need ~38 GB, about what is free.
nodes.notes: Database view: an LRU buffer pool smaller than the working set.

nodes.label: Expert file
nodes.desc: A miss is a page fault: one 4 KB page at a time, ~2.5 GB/s, while the CPU waits.

nodes.label: N-gram table
nodes.desc: Qwen 4's lookup memory. Stock llama.cpp marks it 'lazy' and reads rows on demand. In the first run of the day the box took ~485 page faults per token and prompts crawled at ~28 tok/s; later stock runs reached ~23 tok/s and ~170 prompt tok/s with almost no faults.
nodes.notes: Database view: a key-value index, keyed by the last 2-3 tokens.

flows.name: One generated token
flows.desc: Decode: 11 tok/s in the first run of the day, ~23 tok/s once the box settled (same flags).

steps.note: The last token goes in; the router picks 10 experts in each of 48 layers.
The ~16 n-gram table rows for the last tokens are fetched on demand by llama.cpp's lazy reader.
The first layers run on GPU 0: their experts sit in VRAM, a buffer-pool hit.
Hits are cheap: the GPU reads 3 MB experts at ~800 GB/s.
Half the layers hand over to the CPU; the GPUs sit idle meanwhile.
The CPU reads each picked expert from the page cache (~27 GB/s).
Measured: 98.8% of the experts it needs are already in RAM; the rest are page faults, one small read at a time.
Then the token goes back to the GPU for the output. Every layer is a hand-off and a host sync.

flows.name: Reading your prompt
flows.desc: Prefill: ~28 tok/s in the first run, ~170 once settled: page faults decide it.

steps.note: A 2,000-character prompt (~550 tokens) arrives and is cut into batches of 512 tokens.
For each batch, the CPU-tier layers' experts (~38 GB) are copied over PCIe to a GPU for the big matrix math.
That copy re-reads every CPU-tier expert from RAM, once per 512 tokens.
What RAM can't hold comes from the SSD again, every batch: a full table scan per 512 rows.
